title: Linux - SUID, SGID, ACLs, and Sensitive Files
html:
SUID, SGID, ACLs, and Sensitive Files

SUID and SGID change the effective identity of an executed file; ACLs can grant access that ordinary ls -l mode bits do not show. Review both when a user can read, write, or execute more than the apparent owner and group permissions suggest.

Enumerate privileged executables

find / -xdev -type f \( -perm -4000 -o -perm -2000 \) -ls 2>/dev/null
findmnt -no TARGET,OPTIONS
getcap -r / 2>/dev/null

Focus on custom or recently changed executables, unusual owners, and files on writable mounts. A nosuid mount can suppress set-ID behavior; file capabilities are a separate privilege mechanism described in Linux capabilities. Compare a suspicious binary with its package and check what it executes, opens, or loads with elevated identity.

For an unfamiliar root-owned SUID executable that accepts caller input, review a copy of the binary offline for memory-unsafe argument handling and the code path that reaches it. Record the effective-ID behavior and mitigations such as stack canaries, non-executable memory, position-independent code, and address randomization. An unsafe function name or missing mitigation is only a review lead: exploitability depends on the actual input bounds, reachable control flow, and effective identity at the fault. Do not send long arguments to the live privileged executable merely to test for a crash during passive enumeration.

A familiar SUID program can itself be replaced or backdoored. A recent modification time is a lead, not proof: for a specific suspicious packaged binary, resolve its owning package and compare the installed file with package metadata rather than verifying every package during routine enumeration:

dpkg -S /usr/bin/passwd                  # Debian-family: identify the owner
dpkg --verify passwd                     # Verify only that package
rpm -V --noscripts -f /usr/bin/passwd    # RPM-family: owning package, no verify scriptlets

dpkg --verify checks file contents only where the package database has a recorded checksum; RPM also compares metadata such as mode and ownership. Focus on a mismatch for the privileged executable itself: stripped installations can report missing documentation or locale files elsewhere in the same package. Compare a suspect executable with a trusted vendor package and review the exact changed code. Legitimate local changes, absent checksums, and compromised package metadata limit what either command proves. Run neither the suspicious SUID program nor a package verification script as part of passive triage. See the dpkg verification manual and RPM verification manual.

A SUID program that invokes a shell, relative command, or library from a writable path may cross a trust boundary. See SUID shared-library and linker abuse, the PATH guidance, and the user-ID explanation. For known command-specific escapes, check GTFOBins against the exact binary and invocation allowed on the host.

For a set-user-ID executable, distinguish the caller's real UID from the file owner's effective UID: execve(2) leaves the real UID unchanged and copies the effective UID into the saved UID after any set-ID change. system(3) runs its command through /bin/sh -c; the shell selected by that path affects whether a child retains its effective identity. In particular, Bash privileged-mode rules reset a differing effective UID to the real UID when Bash starts without -p. Check the actual helper's UID changes and child invocation, along with its owner, executable access, mount nosuid setting, and process no_new_privs state. A SUID bit or shell call alone does not establish a usable higher-privilege transition.

An unusual root-owned SUID jjs merits a separate file-access review if the current user can execute it. The legacy Nashorn tool can access Java file APIs even when a spawned shell drops an effective UID; confirm the installed JVM's behavior, the effective identity of the file operation, and nosuid/no_new_privs before treating it as a privileged read or write. Oracle removed jjs in JDK 15; an installed path may still be an older or separately packaged build. GTFOBins documents the file APIs, but its sudo examples do not establish SUID behavior for every build. Do not invoke the tool during passive enumeration.

A root-owned SUID gosu executable accessible to a lower-privileged user warrants review: its documented interface accepts a target user and command, but normal container use starts it as root to drop privileges. Verify the installed build's SUID behavior, effective identity and user-namespace mapping, plus nosuid and no_new_privs; container root does not imply host root. A filename or SUID bit alone is not proof of a working transition. See the upstream usage and maintainer's SUID warning. Do not invoke the helper during passive inventory.

A custom set-user-ID backup wrapper may accept a caller-selected path and interpolate it into an archive command passed to system(3). If that path is unquoted in the constructed command, the child shell can apply tilde expansion using HOME, pathname patterns such as ? and *, and newline command separation; rejecting only familiar punctuation in a denylist does not make the path literal. Confirm the exact argument flow, inherited environment, child shell and effective identity, filesystem access, and whether archive output is visible to the caller. The SUID bit, an archive-tool string, or a blocked /root literal alone proves neither disclosure nor code execution. Review a copy of the wrapper offline rather than archiving private files or sending crash inputs during passive enumeration.

Shell command substitution such as $(...) is another possible gap in a metacharacter denylist: even a fixed permitted command prefix can pass a later caller-controlled argument through /bin/sh -c. Verify the exact quoting, parser, and effective identity offline; do not treat a system() string or incomplete denylist alone as execution proof.

The calling process tree also matters. A web worker can install a seccomp filter that restricts UID-changing system calls; seccomp filters pass to children and survive execve. For example, Apache's mpm-itk LimitUIDRange and LimitGIDRange directives can constrain the identities reachable by descendants. Seccomp: 2 in /proc/self/status shows filter mode, not the policy or whether this particular helper can gain its owner's identity. Review the actual invocation's ancestry and effective filter together with its SUID, mount, and no_new_privs conditions; a separate login session may have a different policy, but requires its own valid access path.

A custom SUID executable may invoke a separate, readable Python script. If it actually uses Python 2, input() evaluates the entered expression; Python 3 input() returns text instead. Confirm the wrapper's effective identity, interpreter path and version, script path, and whether untrusted input reaches that call before treating the source line as an execution path. A set-ID bit on the script itself or an input() call without the privileged wrapper does not establish the same boundary. Review the binary's referenced paths and bounded script source without running it during enumeration.

If readable source accompanies an unusual SUID executable, compare each caller-controlled file read's requested byte count with the destination buffer size and inspect later control-flow checks. fread(3) stores the requested items at the supplied pointer; it does not know the destination object's capacity. A size mismatch is a static memory-safety lead, not proof of a usable privilege escalation: confirm that the source matches the installed binary, the caller can supply the input, SUID execution is effective in that context, and the relevant path is reachable. Review a bounded source or binary copy offline rather than sending crash inputs to the privileged program during enumeration.

A custom SUID helper can disclose a protected file without printing its contents. If the caller chooses both a pathname and a regular expression, and the helper returns a visible match count under its effective UID, anchored prefix tests may form a character-by-character oracle. Confirm the helper's owner, effective-ID behavior, executable access, pathname restrictions, regex semantics, response visibility, and a specific higher-privilege file the caller cannot otherwise read. A SUID bit or regex library string alone proves none of that flow. During passive enumeration, record the unusual executable and review a bounded disassembly or source copy; do not run iterative guesses against the live helper or print recovered secrets.

On OpenBSD, a custom set-user-ID reader that accepts a caller-selected pathname may expose files under /var/backups if its effective identity can read them and it returns their contents to the caller. OpenBSD's changelist(5) describes .current and .backup copies of configured paths, but entries prefixed with + store SHA-256 checksums rather than file contents; the backup directory should be root-owned and mode 0700. A helper's unveil read rule for /var can permit access beneath that path, but does not itself grant or prove file access. Confirm the actual effective UID, executable permission for the current user, accepted path, backup existence and contents, and any independent authentication requirements before claiming escalation. Passive enumeration should report the helper and path metadata, not invoke the reader or print backup data.

A custom SUID program that checks a caller-selected pathname with stat(2) and opens the pathname later can race a change to a file or symlink in a caller-writable directory. The check applies to the earlier object, while a later open(2) may resolve another one. Confirm the helper is executable with elevated effective identity, that an otherwise reachable code path reads the selected file, and that the caller can replace the pathname between check and open; a SUID bit, writable directory, or stat string alone establishes none of these. A visible output or caller-readable destination is also needed for a disclosure path. Review the binary and path metadata offline; do not race the live helper during passive enumeration.

Apply the same dependency review to SGID wrappers. A wrapper that runs a shell or helper by an absolute path can still be unsafe if a lower-privileged user can replace that file; the spawned code may inherit the wrapper's effective group. Check the exact invoked path, its write access (including ACLs), the wrapper's effective group, and whether it drops privileges before launching the child. An interpreter may also discard inherited effective IDs, so distinguish a review candidate from a demonstrated transition. A writable shell elsewhere on the host alone does not prove that a privileged wrapper calls it.

Privileged wrappers that pass SQL to the SQLite CLI

If a custom SUID program passes user-controlled SQL to the sqlite3 command-line program, inspect the exact command and effective identity before treating its query as read-only. The CLI's edit() SQL function invokes an editor (from its second argument or VISUAL), and its SQL load_extension() function can load a shared library when extension loading is enabled. These are potential code-execution paths at the CLI process's identity even if the wrapper fixes PATH or uses an absolute sqlite3 path. The SQL must actually reach those functions, and the CLI must retain the relevant feature; merely finding sqlite3 in a binary or on the host is not evidence of an escalation. The SQLite library disables extension loading by default, so distinguish it from the CLI. Where a privileged application must process untrusted SQL, SQLite's CLI --safe mode disables edit(), load_extension(), and other side-effectful functions. See the SQLite CLI documentation, safe-mode documentation, and extension-loading documentation.

Privileged file readers that feed a verbose client

A custom SUID/SGID wrapper may check access to a caller-selected pathname and then pass that file to another command. Review the effective identity at both the access check and the later open, resolve any ../ components against the real base directory, and inspect how the child handles invalid input. If a database client reads a private file as SQL with verbose output, it may echo the file's contents in errors even though the SQL is invalid. This is a cross-user disclosure only when the child can read a file that the caller cannot, the caller can select that file through the wrapper, and the output is visible; the presence of mysql or another client string alone proves none of these conditions.

Netdata ndsudo search path

CVE-2024-32019 affected some Netdata ndsudo builds. The root-owned SUID helper searched for its permitted external commands using a caller-supplied PATH. Review an installed helper, including one outside the caller's usual PATH, only when the current account can execute it. Confirm its owner, SUID bit, executable access (including group/ACL grants), installed build and vendor patch status, and whether NoNewPrivs or a nosuid mount blocks the identity change. Netdata lists patched builds v1.45.3 and v1.45.0-169; distribution backports need separate confirmation. A dashboard version or the mere presence of ndsudo is insufficient evidence of a reachable escalation. The path issue also requires the helper to resolve an external command through a location the caller controls.

Firejail join privilege boundary

CVE-2022-31214 affected Firejail's privileged --join logic: a crafted join target could make the setuid-root helper accept an attacker-controlled mount namespace and copy unsafe security state. For passive triage, confirm that the current identity can execute a root-owned setuid Firejail binary, that setuid is effective on its mount and in its process context, and that the installed build lacks the fix. Upstream fixed the issue in 0.9.70; distribution packages may backport it while still displaying an older version. Those prerequisites identify a review candidate, not a successful join or root shell. Do not construct a fake jail or invoke --join during enumeration.

GNU Screen logfile permissions

CVE-2017-5618 involved Screen 4.5.0 opening a caller-chosen logfile with elevated privileges. A screen or version-suffixed binary in the SUID inventory is only a review lead: confirm root ownership, effective SUID execution for the current user, the installed build and distribution patch status, and the affected logfile behavior. Debian fixed its 4.5.0 package with a backport, so a version string or filename alone does not prove exposure. Do not create a logfile as a routine enumeration probe.

CVE-2017-5899 affected the privileged S-nail mail-lock helper when a caller-controlled path component could traverse directories and lead to an arbitrary file write. Review whether the current user can execute an installed root-owned setuid helper, whether its setuid identity is effective under the mount and process policy, and the exact package build and vendor fix. Ubuntu's security notice lists a backported fix for its 16.04 package, so an upstream-looking version alone is inconclusive. Helper presence does not prove that the affected path is reachable or that a file write yields root execution; inspect metadata and package status without invoking the helper or attempting the race during enumeration.

snap-confine and tmpfiles cleanup

CVE-2026-3888 is a race involving privileged snap-confine and systemd-tmpfiles cleanup of /tmp. A passive review can check whether snap-confine is setuid or has file capabilities, compare the installed snapd package with the fixed version for that Ubuntu release, and inspect the effective /tmp age rule and cleanup timer. A matching package and rule are prerequisites, not proof that the race is reachable: runtime timer state, snap layout, package backports, and rule overrides also matter. Older releases may require non-default configuration. Do not run a race probe during routine enumeration. See the Ubuntu CVE record for release-specific package status and the Qualys advisory for the component interaction.

Inspect ACLs and sensitive paths

getfacl -p /path/to/file /path/to/parent 2>/dev/null
namei -l /path/to/file
find /etc /opt /var -type f -writable -ls 2>/dev/null | head -80
ls -la /etc/sudoers.d /etc/ld.so.preload /etc/ld.so.conf.d 2>/dev/null

A writable parent directory may permit replacement even when the file itself is root-owned. An ACL may quietly grant access to a sudoers drop-in, service unit, cron script, library path, or credential file. Check both the ACL and the full path. If arbitrary privileged file writes are possible, follow Arbitrary File Write to Root; for linker configuration and preload cases, see the ld.so example. Treat exposed backups, .env files, database configs, SSH material, and history as possible credential sources, with access governed by the actual permissions of each file.
